overview:
Any ox, lamb, or goat an Israelite slaughters must be brought to the door of the tabernacle and offered there as a peace offering; a man who kills one anywhere else is charged with shedding blood. Every burnt offering and sacrifice, from Israelite or stranger, goes to the same door. No one may eat blood. A hunter who catches game must pour out its blood and cover it with dust, and anyone who eats an animal found dead or torn must wash.

The reason sits at the center, in v. 11: “the life of the flesh is in the blood.” Because blood is life, it has only two proper places. It goes on the altar, where God has given it “to make an atonement for your souls,” or into the ground under dust. It never goes into the mouth.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses; many scholars assign Leviticus to a priestly writer or school.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses' lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); scholarly proposals reach the 6th–5th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Given at Sinai while Israel camped around the newly raised tabernacle (Exodus 40:17; Numbers 1:1). Traditional Exodus date about 1446 BC; many scholars prefer the 13th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: A camp in the wilderness, with one altar at the tent door and open country beyond it, “in the camp, or … out of the camp” (v. 3).

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Genesis 9:4 forbids blood to Noah's descendants; Leviticus 7:26–27 and 19:26 repeat the ban. Deuteronomy 12:15–24 relaxes the place of slaughter but keeps the blood rule.

hermeneutics:
Across the ancient world, blood was food for spirits. In Homer's *Odyssey* (book 11), Odysseus digs a trench, cuts the throats of two sheep so the blood runs in, and the ghosts swarm up from below; the prophet Teiresias must drink before he can speak. Hurrian and Hittite rituals opened pits for the gods of the underworld, and the victim's blood was smeared on the rim or run down into the hole, as excavated pits at Urkesh in Syria bear out. Against that background the chapter's rules have an edge. Blood left open on the ground could feed whatever lived below. Leviticus sends it to the altar or covers it with dust (v. 13), and v. 7 names the alternative: sacrifices in the open field to “devils,” Hebrew *se'irim*, literally “goats,” the satyrs of Isaiah 13:21.

Israel also believed that uncovered blood cries out. Abel's blood cries to God from the ground (Genesis 4:10). Job pleads, “O earth, cover not thou my blood” (Job 16:18), so that his case stays open. Ezekiel charges Jerusalem with setting blood on a bare rock instead of covering it with dust, so that it calls for vengeance (Ezekiel 24:7–8). That explains the hard words of v. 4. A man who kills an ox away from the altar has not returned its life to God, and so “he hath shed blood,” the language used of killing a person.

breakdown.label: To Aaron, his sons, and all Israel
Slaughter only at the tent door, not to goat-demons
Every offering, from Israelite or stranger, at the same door
No eating blood: the life is in the blood
Hunted game: pour out the blood and cover it
Animals found dead or torn: washing required

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence, five short laws with the reason for them at v. 11.
notes: **Same opening:** laws 1–4 each begin with the doubled Hebrew *ish ish*, “whatsoever man” (vv. 3, 8, 10, 13). From v. 8 on, each also names “the strangers which sojourn among you.”
**Blood:** the word *dam* occurs 13 times in 16 verses, three times in v. 14 alone.
**Cut off:** the penalty “cut off” comes four times (vv. 4, 9, 10, 14), once in each of the first four laws. The fifth law, on carcasses, ends instead with bearing iniquity (v. 16).

Ch. 17 opens the last large block of the book, chs. 17–26, which scholars since 1877 call the Holiness Code after its refrain “ye shall be holy” (19:2; 20:7, 26). The block ends with the summary at 26:46. The chapter's subject, blood, ties it back to ch. 16, where blood cleanses the sanctuary.

**Later echoes:** Saul's hungry troops slaughter on the ground and eat “with the blood,” and Saul has a great stone rolled up to slaughter on (1 Samuel 14:32–34). Deuteronomy 12:15–24 allows slaughter far from the sanctuary but says to pour the blood out “as water.”

traditions.text: The JST expands the blood command given to Noah. The blood of all flesh given for meat is to be shed upon the ground and not eaten, blood is not to be shed except for meat to save life, and God will require the blood of every beast at man's hands. It gives the rule of Leviticus 17 a setting long before Sinai, as Jubilees also does.

The Lord says that beasts and fowls are ordained for man's food and clothing, so forbidding meat is not of God. The same passage adds a limit: a woe on the man who sheds blood “or that wasteth flesh and hath no need.” Like Leviticus 17, it treats the killing of an animal as something God takes account of, even when the meat is lawful to eat.

Amulek foresees that the great and last sacrifice will bring a stop to the shedding of blood and fulfill the law of Moses. After his resurrection, Christ's voice tells the Nephites to offer him no more the shedding of blood, but “a broken heart and a contrite spirit.” Verse 11 gives blood to Israel upon the altar to atone; these passages describe that use of blood ending.

Jubilees traces the blood law to Noah, who with his sons swore never to eat blood, and says it is written on the heavenly tablets with no limit of days. Moses is told to command Israel to eat no blood, so that the blood of their offerings may seek forgiveness for them before the altar. Verse 11's two ideas, no blood eaten and blood for atonement, are already joined here.

Summarizing the law for Greek readers, Josephus says Moses forbade blood as food altogether and “esteemed it to contain the soul and spirit.” He puts v. 11's “life” in the terms Greek readers would know, soul and spirit, and in the same breath forbids the flesh of an animal that died of itself, the case v. 15 treats, and the fat of goats, sheep, and bulls.

The rabbis worked out v. 13 as a standing duty. Covering the blood applies in the land of Israel and abroad, with or without a temple, to wild animals and birds but not to domestic cattle or to sacrifices. Because it does not depend on the altar, the rule outlived the temple, and observant Jews still cover the blood of slaughtered fowl and game with dust or earth.

On v. 7 Rashi, following the Sifra, takes *se'irim* as demons and points to the same word in Isaiah 13:21. On v. 11 he says the life of every creature, not only sacrificial animals, depends on its blood, so God set blood on the altar to atone for human life: “let life come and expiate for life.” On v. 13 he notes that the verb “hunteth” teaches a person to eat meat only after some toil in preparing it.

The Jerusalem council asks Gentile believers to abstain from things offered to idols, from blood, from things strangled, and from fornication. Many interpreters connect the list with Leviticus 17–18, the laws that bind “the stranger” as well as Israel. James had just noted that Moses is read in the synagogues every sabbath, and many readers take that as the reason for the list: shared tables with Jewish believers.

Hebrews says that under the law almost everything is cleansed with blood, and “without shedding of blood is no remission.” It is a summary of v. 11's principle, which Hebrews then applies to the blood of Christ.

Answering the charge that Christians drank human blood, Tertullian says they do not even have the blood of animals at their meals and avoid things strangled or dead of themselves. Persecutors, he says, tempted Christians with blood sausages, knowing they would refuse. Over a century after Acts 15, the blood rule was still a mark of Christian practice in North Africa.

traditions.source: Letter of the churches of Vienne and Lyons, in Eusebius
traditions.text: During the persecution at Lyons, a woman named Biblis, who had at first denied Christ, turned on her torturers. She asked how people who think it unlawful to taste even the blood of animals could eat children, then confessed herself a Christian. Her answer shows the same practice Tertullian describes in another province.
